MEMFD.name: code from a file that exists only in memory
MEMFD.en: executable mapping of a memfd (file that exists only in RAM)
MEMFD.meaning: The process executes code from a file created with the memfd_create call. Such a file exists only in RAM and is never written to disk.
MEMFD.why: This is a popular way on Linux to run a program without writing it to disk: a downloaded executable is placed in a memfd and launched from there.
MEMFD.tech: Executable mapping of an object created by memfd_create (a /memfd:<name> entry in /proc/<pid>/maps).

DEL-EXEC.name: code from a file deleted from disk
DEL-EXEC.en: executable mapping of a file deleted from disk
DEL-EXEC.meaning: The program runs code from a file that has already been deleted from disk. The code keeps running because the system retains the file for as long as something is using it.
DEL-EXEC.why: Deleting the file after launch is a simple way to cover tracks: the program can no longer be found or examined on disk.
DEL-EXEC.tech: Executable mapping of a file marked (deleted) in /proc/<pid>/maps: the directory entry has been removed, the inode remains in use.

X-TMP.name: code from a temporary directory
X-TMP.en: executable mapping of a file that lives in a world-writable directory such as /tmp or /dev/shm (Linux); legitimate software that unpacks native libraries there also triggers it
X-TMP.meaning: The program runs code from a file located in a directory that any user can write to (e.g. /tmp, /dev/shm).
X-TMP.why: Temporary directories are the first place an attacker writes downloaded tools to, because they require no privileges.
X-TMP.tech: Executable mapping of an existing file from /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /run/shm, /run/user, /var/lock, /run/lock or /dev/mqueue.

RWX.tech: Mapping with rwx permissions in /proc/<pid>/maps (PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE and PROT_EXEC at the same time).

X-PRIV.tech: Executable mapping with no file path in /proc/<pid>/maps (anonymous memory), excluding kernel regions ([vdso] and similar).

THR-PRIV.tech: The instruction address from /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/syscall points to a memory region not backed by a file. Only threads waiting in a system call are assessed.

IMG-MOD.tech: Executable, non-writable file mapping with a non-zero Anonymous field in /proc/<pid>/smaps (pages copied on write).

SHC.tech: Search in executable regions without a plain file (anonymous memory and memfd; files on disk, deleted ones included, are not examined): on x86_64 a direct execve call, finding its own address (call/pop, fnstenv), the prologue of known loader stages and patterns of Windows code run under Wine; on arm64 the svc instruction.

combos.title: encrypted or packed code from a file that exists only in memory
combos.meaning: Code is executed from a file that exists only in RAM, and its content appears random.
benign: Rare. Some runtimes and sandboxes use memfd, but their code does not look encrypted.
malicious: A program downloaded from the network and run without being written to disk, and additionally packed. This is the typical picture of fileless malware on Linux.

combos.title: code from a file that exists only in memory
combos.meaning: Code is executed from a memfd file that is not present on disk.
benign: JIT runtimes that use dual memory mapping, browser sandboxes, some graphics drivers.
malicious: Fileless execution of a downloaded program.

combos.title: code from a file deleted from disk
combos.meaning: A library or program is still running although its file is no longer on disk.
benign: Package update: an old version of a library has been replaced by a new one and the program has not been restarted yet. In that case the path usually points to a system directory.
malicious: A program launched and deleted immediately to hinder analysis. In that case the path often points to a temporary or home directory.

combos.title: code from a temporary directory
combos.meaning: The program loaded an executable file from a world-writable directory.
benign: Programs that unpack their own libraries to /tmp: Java applications with native libraries, programs packaged with PyInstaller, AppImage images.
malicious: A tool downloaded by an attacker and run from /tmp or /dev/shm.

combos.title: standalone code in a file that exists only in memory
combos.meaning: An executable file that exists only in memory (memfd) contains sequences typical of code that works without the help of the program loader, for example starting another program directly through the kernel.
benign: A container runtime that copies its own program into a file in memory before starting; such a program calls the kernel itself.
A statically compiled program started from a file in memory by a deployment tool.
malicious: A program downloaded from the network and started without being written to disk.
A payload that starts a shell with a direct system call.

hints.text: The process contains a just-in-time (JIT) runtime ({runtime}); it may keep generated code in a file in memory, but it does not explain starting programs directly. Check the name of the memfd file and the code at the address from the finding description.
No just-in-time (JIT) runtime was recognised in the process; copy the memfd file (the step for the MEMFD feature) and check what program it is.

*.do: See what this memory region is in the process memory map
*.look: The output is one line: address range, permissions (e.g. r-xp, the letter x means executable code) and, at the end, a file path. Benign case: the line ends with the path of a library or program in a system directory such as /usr/lib. Be concerned if there is no path (memory not backed by a file), a memfd: entry, a (deleted) note, or a path in /tmp or /dev/shm together with the letter x in the permissions: in that case save the region to a file (next step).

*.do: Save the memory region content to a file (requires gdb, pauses the process briefly)
*.look: Expected result: the command ends without an error and a file /tmp/region_... appears, with a size equal to the size of the region. The messages "Operation not permitted" or "Cannot access memory" mean missing permissions (run as root) or that the region no longer exists: on their own they do not indicate a threat. The saved file is the input for the next steps and a piece of evidence, do not run it.

*.do: Check who started the process and with what command
*.look: Look at the columns PPID (parent process), USER, STARTED (start time) and CMD (command). Benign case: the user and the command fit the role of this server, and PPID is 1 (systemd) or a known service manager. Be concerned if the command was started from /tmp or /dev/shm, if a shell (sh, bash) was started by a web server or a database, or if the start time matches the suspected incident: in that case check the parent process with the same command, using its PPID.

HDR.do: After saving the memory region, check what kind of executable file it is
HDR.look: If file prints the word ELF (the format of Linux programs) and readelf shows a header without errors (fields Type, Machine, Entry point address), the region holds a whole program or library loaded without a file on disk, which suggests code loaded straight into memory. If file prints only "data" and readelf reports an error, it is just a fragment or an accidental resemblance and the finding is weaker. In the first case compute the file hash (sha256sum), keep the file as evidence and hand it over for analysis.

ENT-X.do: After saving the memory region, compute its SHA-256 hash and compare it against databases of known files
ENT-X.look: The output is 64 hexadecimal characters (the hash, a fingerprint of the file): look it up in the file reputation database your organization uses, searching by the hash only, without uploading the file. No match is typical for a memory dump and settles nothing, while a match flagged as malicious suggests known malware. On a malicious match, or when other findings concern the same process, keep the file and hand it over for analysis.

MEMFD.do: Find the memfd file descriptor (a file that exists only in memory) and copy the whole file, replacing NUMBER with the descriptor number from the first command
MEMFD.look: The first command prints lines like "5 -> /memfd:name (deleted)": the number before the arrow is the descriptor number, and the (deleted) note is normal here. Benign case: the name points to a known use, e.g. graphics or sound buffers in programs with a graphical interface. Be concerned about an empty or random name in a server process: in that case check the copied file with the file command, and if it prints ELF (a program), this is consistent with running code without writing it to disk, so keep the file and hand it over for analysis.

DEL-EXEC.do: Recover the deleted program file while the process is still running (for a library, copy the matching entry from the map_files directory of this process in /proc instead)
DEL-EXEC.look: Expected result: the copy is created without an error; once the process ends, recovery is no longer possible. Benign case: the program or library comes from a system directory and was updated recently, so the process is simply still running the old version. Be concerned about a file that was located in /tmp, /dev/shm or a home directory and is unrelated to an update, because this is consistent with a program deleting itself after start: in that case compute the hash of the copy (sha256sum) and keep it as evidence.

X-TMP.do: Check the file owner, date and hash, replacing FILE with the file path from the memory region table
X-TMP.look: Look at the owner (third column), the modification date and the hash (64 hexadecimal characters). Benign case: the file belongs to a user who knowingly runs the program and the date fits its start, since some programs (e.g. Java, Python) unpack their libraries into /tmp. Be concerned if the owner is a service account (e.g. www-data), the date matches the suspected incident, or the hash is flagged as malicious in a file reputation database: in that case copy the file as evidence before it disappears.

RWX.do: Check whether the program has a JIT runtime (a mechanism that creates code while running, e.g. Java, Node.js, .NET)
RWX.look: If the command prints lines with the names of such libraries, the program creates code in memory itself, and a region that is both writable and executable is usually normal for it. No output means none of the typical JIT runtimes was found (the list is not complete), so such a region is harder to explain and is consistent with injected code. In that case save the region to a file and check it with the file and sha256sum commands.

THR-PRIV.do: See what the threads of the process are doing (call stack of all threads, pauses the process briefly)
THR-PRIV.look: For each thread a list of frames is printed, in the form "#0 0x... in function () from /path/of/library". Benign case: the frames have a function name and a library path. Be concerned about frames with only an address and "?? ()" without a library, especially at the bottom of the list (the start of the thread), if the address lies within the range of the region from the finding, because this suggests a thread running code from memory not backed by a file ("??" alone can also result from missing symbols): in that case save that region to a file.

IMG-MOD.do: Compare the code in memory with the file: save the memory region (command above) and compare it with the corresponding part of the library file (the offset is in /proc/{pid}/maps)
IMG-MOD.look: Benign case: no differences, or the library file on disk is newer than the process (updated after it started), which explains the mismatch. Be concerned about a few changed bytes at the start of functions, usually a jump to another place in memory (a so-called hook, a redirect of the function), because this is consistent with overwritten library code. In that case note which functions the differences concern, keep the saved region and hand it over for analysis.

SHC.do: After saving the memory region to a file, look at the instructions at the address from the finding description (the address after the @ sign); on arm64 replace i386:x86-64 with aarch64
SHC.look: Search the output for the address from the finding description. Starting a program directly is the number 0x3b put into the rax register (push 0x3b and pop rax, or mov eax,0x3b) followed a few instructions later by syscall; on arm64 it is mov x8 with a number and svc. Code finding its own address is a call to the next instruction followed at once by pop. Benign case: ordinary, long function code around it, and the program is a runtime that generates code or a container runtime. Be concerned about a short fragment that prepares a string such as /bin/sh and calls the kernel right away: in that case keep the file and go to the next step.

SHC.do: Print the strings from the saved region that look like paths and network addresses
SHC.look: An empty result settles nothing, because payloads often build their strings only at run time. Shell paths (/bin/sh, /bin/bash), network addresses or URLs in a region with no file are consistent with a payload that starts a shell or connects to a server: note them, compute the hash of the file (sha256sum) and hand the file over for analysis.

terms./proc: the directory in which Linux exposes information about running processes; the tool only reads from it
terms.memfd: a file created in RAM with the memfd_create call; it is not present on disk
terms.ELF: the format of executables and libraries on Linux; it starts with the bytes 7f 45 4c 46
terms.vdso: a small piece of kernel code inserted into every process; it is normal
terms.capabilities: parts of administrator privileges granted to a process individually; the CapEff field shows the active ones
terms.seccomp: a filter that restricts the system calls a process can make; when enabled, the program is running in a sandbox
terms.LD_PRELOAD: a variable that forces the specified library to be loaded before all others; sometimes used to replace functions

flags.traced by: another process has debugger control (ptrace) over this program; outside of debugging this is rare and worth explaining
flags.effective capabilities: 0000000000000000 means no additional privileges; all hexadecimal ones (e.g. 000001ffffffffff) means full administrator privileges
flags.seccomp: "filter" means the program runs in a sandbox, which limits the impact of a possible compromise
flags.no_new_privs: 1 means the program and its descendants cannot gain higher privileges
flags.root directory: the program sees a different root directory than the system; this usually indicates a container
flags.env LD_PRELOAD: an additional library was injected into the program at startup; check what this file is
flags.env LD_AUDIT: a library that supervises code loading was attached to the program; outside of diagnostic tools this is rare
flags.env LD_LIBRARY_PATH: the program searches for libraries in non-standard directories; if they point to a temporary or home directory, check the contents

handles.file: regular file opened by the program
handles.memfd: file that exists only in RAM
handles.pipe: channel for exchanging data with another process
handles.anon: kernel object, e.g. an event counter

processes.what: The program that manages system startup and services; process number 1 is the ancestor of all others.
SSH remote login server. Its child processes are the sessions of logged-in users.
A shell, i.e. the command line. In itself it is an ordinary tool; what matters is who started it and what it started.
A service that runs tasks at scheduled times. Programs started by cron run without user involvement.
Web server. A shell or interpreter started by a web server is a typical trace of an intrusion through a web application.
Scripting language interpreter. It runs arbitrary code, so the command line and the parent process are what count.
JavaScript runtime with just-in-time (JIT) compilation; writable and executable regions are normal in it.
Java virtual machine with just-in-time (JIT) compilation; writable and executable regions are normal in it.
Part of the container runtime. Processes in containers have their own root directory and their own network.
Test program of the Nanshe tool. It deliberately creates in memory the patterns the detectors look for; it does not execute any of them.

modules.what: core system library; almost every program has it
the program that loads libraries at startup; normal in every process
encryption library; the program is able to establish encrypted connections
library for retrieving data from the network (HTTP and others)
Java virtual machine; generates code just in time (JIT)
V8 JavaScript engine; generates code just in time (JIT)
.NET runtime; generates code just in time (JIT)
Python interpreter embedded in the program
user login library; the program checks passwords or opens sessions
library for resolving user and host names
file that exists only in RAM; it is not present on disk
startup image of the V8 JavaScript engine; present in applications built on Electron and in Chromium-based browsers
modules.family: an application built on the Chromium browser engine, most often on Electron: a windowed program whose interface is a web page shown by an embedded browser. It runs as several processes of the same file and generates code at run time.

modules.what: the Chromium browser engine as shipped in Qt WebEngine; generates code at run time
modules.family: a program that uses Qt WebEngine: a Qt application that shows web content with an embedded Chromium engine. Pages are usually handled by a separate QtWebEngineProcess process, which generates code at run time.
